messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eli, a 63-year-old rabbi, had built his life around guiding a small congregation in a quiet Midwestern town. Twenty-three years earlier, he had fled a country where his religious community was systematically targeted. One night, armed men stormed his home while his family was at dinner. He remembered the shouting—vicious, guttural—and the sudden, unforgiving grip of a hand on his shoulder that spun him around. A rifle butt slammed into his ribs. He watched his wife and children being herded outside, and in that moment he froze, unable to act. He later learned that neighbors had been killed, and he carried the belief that any other man would have found a way to stop it. That single, unexpected touch—the hand on his shoulder—had become engraved in his nervous system.

Now, in his new life, Eli felt trapped by his body. A worshipper coming up behind him and touching his arm during a blessing would send his heart racing before he could even think. Shouting during a heated committee meeting made his chest tighten, and once, when a teenager brought a toy gun to a youth event, Eli had to excuse himself, trembling. Each time a trigger occurred, he told himself he deserved to suffer for what happened that night—that his cowardice meant he should not feel safe. He had come to believe his body was the enemy, flooding him with panic long after any real danger was gone. This conviction meant that ordinary sensations—a sudden tap on his shoulder, a raised voice—now carried the weight of the attack itself, making each one a fresh reminder of his failure. That appraisal, in turn, made him see threats everywhere. He chose his seat at every meeting and Shabbat dinner—back against the wall, door in clear view—to feel remotely protected. Only in his study at the synagogue and in his living room at home did he feel even close to safe, and he rarely left those two zones.

The constant vigilance wore on him. He had difficulty concentrating during sermons, losing his train of thought when someone shifted in their seat. This only confirmed his belief that he could not rely on himself. If another man, any other man, would have stopped the attack, then Eli was fundamentally broken. That thought made the world feel more dangerous, and so his attention narrowed even further to potential threats. The cycle tightened: his threat-driven scanning caught every accidental touch, every raised voice, confirming his negative appraisals. To manage, he distracted himself—immersing in Talmudic arguments or watching hours of news he barely absorbed. But the distraction itself left him feeling that he could not face his own mind, confirming his belief that he was too weak to confront what had happened. He also began avoiding emotional closeness with his wife, Rebecca, pulling away from her hand on his arm or deflecting when she wanted to talk about their past. The punishment thinking—that he deserved to suffer—made him feel that intimacy was a grace he had forfeited. And yet his avoidance made the triggers worse: the less contact he tolerated, the more startling each unanticipated touch became.

In recent months, Rebecca had confronted him, saying she felt like a stranger in her own marriage. Eli realized his strategies were unraveling the life he had rebuilt. He came to therapy wary and exhausted, haunted by the suspicion that he would never be the man he should have been. What frightened him most was not the memories, but the quiet certainty that he was unworthy of relief.
